Summarizing and Visualizing Two Numeric Variables

Scatter Plots

Scatter Plots

Definition: Scatter Plot

Suppose you have a data matrix containing \(n\) cases and numeric variables \(x\) and \(y\) measured on each case. A scatter plot for these two variables is simply a graph containing a circle or dot at each point \((x_i, y_i)\), so there is exactly one dot for each case in the data matrix.

Trend Lines

Trends and Noise

In the previous scatter plot, we saw that there was an upward trend: More customers are associated with longer waits.

We also saw that the trend is imperfect: The points are scattered around the trend line. We call this additional scattering noise.

The decomposition of data into trend plus noise is the most important idea in statistics.

Trends and Regression

Defining the Trend

What is a trend?

It is easy to sketch a trend line through data, but each person might sketch a slightly different line. In order to have objective measures of trend and noise, and in order to communicate clearly, we need a precise, objective definition of the trend line.

Defining the Trend

Step 1: Equation for the trend.

Equation for a line

Recall that every line can be written using an intercept \(a\) and a slope \(b\):

\[ y = a + bx \]

To define the trend line, we need to define \(a\) and \(b\).

Defining the Trend

Step 2: Define the noise.

Definition: Predictions and Residuals

Let \(x\) and \(y\) be variables in a data matrix with trend line \(y = a + bx\). For any value \(x_i\) in the data matrix, we define the predicted value of \(y\) by

\[ \hat{y}_i = a+bx_i \]

The gap between the predicted and actual value of \(y\) is called the residual and is defined by:

\[ e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i \]

Predictions and Residuals

Scatter Plot with Predictions and Residuals

The grey vertical lines show the residuals

The orange dots on the line show the predictions

A Note on Terminology

The predicted values \(\hat{y}_i\) represent the trend.

The residuals represent the noise.

If there were no noise, we would have:

  • predicted = actual
  • residuals = 0

Defining the Trend

Step 3: Minimize the residuals

Rough Definition: Best Fit Line

To define the trend line, we can ask for the line that best fits the data, meaning that the noise is as small as possible. This means we should try to minimize the size of the residuals for each predicted value.

Detour: How Much Error?

Warning

We cannot minimize every residual simultaneously. A line that perfectly predicts the \(y\) value of the first data point might do a horrible job predicting the second. Therefore, we want to make residuals small while balancing them across the whole dataset.

Detour: How Much Error?

We can measure the error of a possible trend line \(y=a + bx\) as the mean of squared residuals:

\[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - (a + bx_i)\right)^2 \]

Defining the Trend

Step 3: Minimize the residuals

Definition: Best Fit Line

The best fit line is the line with intercept \(a\) and slope \(b\) that minimize the average squared residual, i.e. 

\[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - (a + bx_i)\right)^2 \]

The Best Fit Line: Notes

  • Best fit line is the “closest” line to the data
  • The best line is not necessarily a good line
    • Best fit line can have large average squared residual
    • This happens when \(x\) does not explain \(y\) well
  • Best fit line is usually called the regression line

A Note on Nonlinearity

Sometimes the data has a trend that isn’t described well by a straight line:

A nonlinear pattern in data

A Note on Nonlinearity

A nonlinear pattern in data

In this case, the best fitting line is the wrong description of the data.

People often fit lines to data without paying attention to whether a straight line is appropriate.
